subQuestions.questionText:
Truck drivers travel a certain distance and have a rest before travelling further. A driver kept record of the distance he travelled (in km) on 8 trips and the amount of time he rested (in minutes) before he continued his journey. The information is given in the table below.

| Distance travelled (in km) $x$ | 180 | 200 | 400 | 600 | 170 | 350 | 270 | 300 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amount of rest time (in minutes) $y$ | 20 | 25 | 55 | 120 | 15 | 50 | 40 | 45 |

Determine the equation of the least squares regression line for the data.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $a = -23{,}846\ldots$
Mark 2: $b = 0{,}227\ldots$
Mark 3: Equation — $\hat{y} = -23{,}85 + 0{,}23x$

subQuestions.questionText: If a truck driver travelled $550$ km, predict the amount of time (in minutes) that he should rest before continuing his journey.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution of 550 — $\hat{y} = -23{,}85 + 0{,}23(550)$
Mark 2: Answer — $y = 102{,}65$ (or $y = 101{,}02$ using the calculator's unrounded coefficients)

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the correlation coefficient for the data.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $r = 0{,}98$

subQuestions.questionText: Interpret your answer to QUESTION 1.3.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: (Very) strong positive correlation

subQuestions.questionText:
At each stop, the truck driver spent money buying food and other refreshments. The amount spent (in rands) is given in the table below.

| 100 | 150 | 130 | 200 | 50 | 180 | 200 | 190 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Calculate the mean amount of money he spent at each stop.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $\bar{x} = \dfrac{1200}{8}$
Mark 2: $\bar{x} = 150$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the standard deviation for the data.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: $\sigma = 50{,}50$

subQuestions.questionText: At how many stops did the driver spend an amount that was less than one standard deviation below the mean?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Calculation of $\bar{x} - \sigma = 150 - 50{,}50 = 99{,}50$
Mark 2: Answer — 1 stop (only R50 is below R99,50)

subQuestions.questionText:
At a certain school, the staff committee wanted to determine how many glasses of water the staff members drank during a school day. All teachers present on a specific day were interviewed. The information is shown in the table below.

| Number of glasses of water drank per day | Number of staff members |
|---|---|
| $0 \leq x < 2$ | 5 |
| $2 \leq x < 4$ | 15 |
| $4 \leq x < 6$ | 13 |
| $6 \leq x < 8$ | 5 |
| $8 \leq x < 10$ | 2 |

Complete the cumulative frequency column provided in the table in the ANSWER BOOK.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Cumulative frequencies 5; 20; 33 — $5\,;\,20\,;\,33$
Mark 2: 38; 40 — final cumulative frequency $40$

subQuestions.questionText: How many staff members were interviewed?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: 40 staff members

subQuestions.questionText: How many staff members drank fewer than 6 glasses of water during a school day?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: 33 staff members

subQuestions.questionText:
The staff committee observed that $k$ teachers were absent on the day of the interviews. It was found that half of these $k$ teachers drank from 0 to fewer than 2 (that is $0 \leq x < 2$) glasses of water per day, while the remainder of them drank from 4 to fewer than 6 (that is $4 \leq x < 6$) glasses of water per day. When these $k$ teachers are included in the data, the estimated mean is 4 glasses of water per staff member per day.

How many teachers were absent on the day of the interviews?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Set up estimated mean with the extra teachers — $\bar{x} = \dfrac{\left(1\times\left(5+\tfrac{k}{2}\right)\right) + (3\times 15) + \left(5\times\left(13+\tfrac{k}{2}\right)\right) + (7\times 5) + (9\times 2)}{40+k} = 4$
Mark 2: Midpoint term $\left(1\times\left(5+\tfrac{k}{2}\right)\right)$
Mark 3: Midpoint term $\left(5\times\left(13+\tfrac{k}{2}\right)\right)$
Mark 4: Solve — $5+\tfrac{k}{2}+45+65+\tfrac{5k}{2}+35+18 = 160+4k \Rightarrow 3k+168 = 160+4k \Rightarrow k = 8$ teachers
(Alternatively, original estimated mean $= 4{,}2$; $\bar{x}_{\text{old}} - 4 = 0{,}2$; $0{,}2 \times 40 = 8$ teachers.)

subQuestions.questionText:
In the figure, $L(-4\,;\,1)$, $S(4\,;\,5)$ and $N(-2\,;\,-3)$ are the vertices of a triangle having $S\hat{L}N = 90^\circ$. $LN$ intersects the $x$-axis at $K$.

Calculate the length of $SL$. Leave your answer in surd form.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution of S and L into the distance formula — $SL = \sqrt{(4-(-4))^2 + (5-1)^2}$
Mark 2: Answer — $SL = \sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt{5} \; (= 8{,}94)$ units

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the gradient of $SN$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution of S and N into the gradient formula — $m_{SN} = \dfrac{5-(-3)}{4-(-2)}$
Mark 2: Answer — $m_{SN} = \dfrac{4}{3}$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the size of $\theta$, the angle of inclination of $SN$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $\tan\theta = m_{SN} = \dfrac{4}{3}$
Mark 2: $\theta = 53{,}13^\circ$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the size of $L\hat{N}S$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $m_{LN} = \dfrac{1-(-3)}{-4-(-2)} = -2$
Mark 2: Angle of inclination — $L\hat{K}O = 116{,}565\ldots^\circ$
Mark 3: $L\hat{N}S = 116{,}565\ldots^\circ - 53{,}13^\circ = 63{,}44^\circ$
(Alternatively, using $SN = 10$, $LN = 2\sqrt{5}$: $\tan L\hat{N}S = \dfrac{4\sqrt{5}}{2\sqrt{5}} \Rightarrow L\hat{N}S = 63{,}44^\circ$.)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of the line which passes through $L$ and is parallel to $SN$. Write your answer in the form $y = mx + c$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $m = m_{SN} = \dfrac{4}{3}$
Mark 2: Substitution of $m$ and $L(-4\,;\,1)$ — $1 = \dfrac{4}{3}(-4) + c \Rightarrow c = \dfrac{19}{3}$
Mark 3: Equation — $y = \dfrac{4}{3}x + \dfrac{19}{3}$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the area of $\triangle LSN$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $LN = \sqrt{(-4-(-2))^2 + (1-(-3))^2} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}$
Mark 2: Substitution into the area formula — Area $\triangle LSN = \dfrac{1}{2}(4\sqrt{5})(2\sqrt{5})$
Mark 3: Answer — $= 20$ units$^2$
(Alternatively, Area $= \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(2\sqrt{5})\sin 63{,}44^\circ = 20$ units$^2$.)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the coordinates of point $P$, which is equidistant from $L$, $S$ and $N$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $\hat{L} = 90^\circ$, so $SN$ is a diameter of circle $S, L, N$ and $P$ is the midpoint of $SN$ [chord subtends $90^\circ$ / converse $\angle$ in semi-circle]
Mark 2: $x$-value of $P$ — $\dfrac{4+(-2)}{2} = 1$
Mark 3: $y$-value of $P$ — $\dfrac{5+(-3)}{2} = 1$, so $P(1\,;\,1)$
(Alternatively, let $P(a\,;\,b)$: $PL = PN$ and $PS = PN$ give two linear equations solving to $a = 1$, $b = 1$.)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the size of $L\hat{P}S$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $L\hat{P}N = \theta = 53{,}13^\circ$ [alt $\angle$s; $LP \parallel x$-axis]
Mark 2: $L\hat{P}S = 126{,}87^\circ$
(Alternatively, $\angle$ at centre $= 2\times\angle$ at circumference: $L\hat{P}S = 2 \times L\hat{N}S = 126{,}88^\circ$.)

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, the circle with centre $O$ has the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 20$. $G(t\,;\,0)$ is the centre of the larger circle. A common tangent touches the circles at $D$ and $F$ respectively, such that $D(p\,;\,-2)$ lies in the 4th quadrant.

Given that $D(p\,;\,-2)$ lies on the smaller circle, show that $p = 4$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution of $D(p\,;\,-2)$ into $x^2 + y^2 = 20$ — $p^2 + (-2)^2 = 20$
Mark 2: $p^2 = 16 \Rightarrow p = \pm 4$; $p = 4$ (in the 4th quadrant)

subQuestions.questionText: $E(6\,;\,2)$ is the midpoint of $DF$. Determine the coordinates of $F$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Method — $\dfrac{4+x_F}{2} = 6$ and $\dfrac{-2+y_F}{2} = 2$
Mark 2: $x$-value — $x_F = 8$
Mark 3: $y$-value — $y_F = 6$, so $F(8\,;\,6)$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of the common tangent, $DF$, in the form $y = mx + c$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Correct substitution — $m_{DE} = \dfrac{-2-2}{4-6}$
Mark 2: Gradient of $DE$, $DF$ or $EF$ — $m = 2$
Mark 3: Substitution of point $D(4\,;\,-2)$ or $E(6\,;\,2)$ or $F(8\,;\,6)$ — $-2 = 2(4) + c \Rightarrow c = -10$
Mark 4: Answer — $y = 2x - 10$
(Alternatively, $m_{OD} = -\tfrac{1}{2}$, so $m_{DE} = 2$ [tan $\perp$ radius].)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the value of $t$. Show ALL working.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Correct gradient of $GF$ — $m_{GF} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ [tan $\perp$ radius]
Mark 2: Substitution of $F$ — $\dfrac{0-6}{t-8} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow -(t-8) = 2(-6)$
Mark 3: Answer — $t = 20$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of the larger circle in the form $ax^2 + by^2 + cx + dy + e = 0$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution of $F$ and $G$ — $(8-20)^2 + (6-0)^2 = r^2$
Mark 2: Value of $r^2$ — $r^2 = 180$
Mark 3: Equation of circle — $(x-20)^2 + y^2 = 180$
Mark 4: Answer — $x^2 + y^2 - 40x + 220 = 0$

subQuestions.questionText: The smaller circle must be translated by $k$ units along the $x$-axis to touch the larger circle internally. Calculate the possible values of $k$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Radii — smaller circle $r = 2\sqrt{5}$, larger circle $r = 6\sqrt{5}$
Mark 2: Method — with $G(20\,;\,0)$: $k = 20 - (6\sqrt{5} - 2\sqrt{5})$ or $k = 20 + (6\sqrt{5} - 2\sqrt{5})$
Marks 3–4 (double mark): $k = 20 - 4\sqrt{5} = 11{,}06$ units or $k = 20 + 4\sqrt{5} = 28{,}94$ units

subQuestions.questionText:
Given: $\sin\beta = \dfrac{1}{3}$, where $\beta \in (90^\circ\,;\,270^\circ)$.

**Without using a calculator**, determine each of the following:

$\cos\beta$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Use $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ (with $y = 1$, $r = 3$)
Mark 2: $x = -\sqrt{8} = -2\sqrt{2}$ (negative in the given interval)
Mark 3: Answer — $\cos\beta = \dfrac{-2\sqrt{2}}{3}$
(Alternatively, $\cos^2\beta = 1 - \sin^2\beta = \tfrac{8}{9} \Rightarrow \cos\beta = \dfrac{-2\sqrt{2}}{3}$.)

subQuestions.questionText: $\sin 2\beta$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Double angle — $\sin 2\beta = 2\sin\beta\cos\beta$
Mark 2: Substitution — $= 2\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{-\sqrt{8}}{3}\right)$
Mark 3: Answer — $= \dfrac{-2\sqrt{8}}{9} = \dfrac{-4\sqrt{2}}{9}$

subQuestions.questionText: $\cos(450^\circ - \beta)$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: $\cos(450^\circ - \beta) = \cos(90^\circ - \beta)$
Mark 2: Co-ratio — $= \sin\beta$
Mark 3: Answer — $= \dfrac{1}{3}$
(Alternatively, expand $\cos 450^\circ\cos\beta + \sin 450^\circ\sin\beta = \cos 90^\circ\cos\beta + \sin 90^\circ\sin\beta = \sin\beta = \tfrac{1}{3}$.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Given: $\dfrac{\cos^4 x + \sin^2 x\cdot\cos^2 x}{1 + \sin x}$

Prove that $\dfrac{\cos^4 x + \sin^2 x\cdot\cos^2 x}{1 + \sin x} = 1 - \sin x$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1: Common factor — $\text{LHS} = \dfrac{\cos^2 x(\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x)}{1 + \sin x}$
Mark 2: $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$ — $= \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{1 + \sin x}$
Mark 3: $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$ — $= \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{1 + \sin x}$
Mark 4: Factorise and simplify — $= \dfrac{(1-\sin x)(1+\sin x)}{1 + \sin x} = 1 - \sin x = \text{RHS}$

subQuestions.questionText: For what value(s) of $x$ in the interval $x \in [0^\circ\,;\,360^\circ]$ is $\dfrac{\cos^4 x + \sin^2 x\cdot\cos^2 x}{1 + \sin x}$ undefined?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $\sin x + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \sin x = -1$ (ref. $\angle = 90^\circ$)
Mark 2: $x = 270^\circ$

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the minimum value of the function defined by $y = \dfrac{\cos^4 x + \sin^2 x\cdot\cos^2 x}{1 + \sin x}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Marks 1–2 (double mark): $y = 1 - \sin x$, so minimum $= 0$

subQuestions.questionText:
Given: $\cos(A - B) = \cos A\cos B + \sin A\sin B$

Use the above identity to deduce that $\sin(A - B) = \sin A\cos B - \cos A\sin B$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Co-ratio — $\sin(A-B) = \cos[90^\circ - (A-B)] = \cos[(90^\circ - A) - (-B)]$
Mark 2: Compound angle — $= \cos(90^\circ - A)\cos(-B) + \sin(90^\circ - A)\sin(-B)$
Mark 3: Reduction — $= \sin A\cos B + \cos A(-\sin B) = \sin A\cos B - \cos A\sin B$

subQuestions.questionText: Hence, or otherwise, determine the general solution of the equation $\sin 48^\circ\cos x - \cos 48^\circ\sin x = \cos 2x$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: Compound angle — $\sin(48^\circ - x) = \cos 2x$
Mark 2: Co-ratio — $\sin(48^\circ - x) = \sin(90^\circ - 2x)$
Mark 3: Both equations — $48^\circ - x = 90^\circ - 2x + k\cdot 360^\circ$ or $48^\circ - x = 180^\circ - (90^\circ - 2x) + k\cdot 360^\circ$
Mark 4: General solution — $x = 42^\circ + k\cdot 360^\circ$
Mark 5: General solution — $x = -14^\circ - k\cdot 120^\circ$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$

subQuestions.questionText: Simplify $\dfrac{\sin 3x + \sin x}{\cos 2x + 1}$ to a single trigonometric ratio.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (6 marks):
Mark 1: Write $3x = (2x + x)$ — $\dfrac{\sin(2x+x) + \sin(2x-x)}{\cos 2x + 1}$
Mark 2: Expansion — $\dfrac{\sin 2x\cos x + \cos 2x\sin x + \sin 2x\cos x - \cos 2x\sin x}{2\cos^2 x - 1 + 1}$
Mark 3: Double angle of $\cos 2x$ — denominator $= 2\cos^2 x$
Mark 4: Simplification — $= \dfrac{2\sin 2x\cos x}{2\cos^2 x}$
Mark 5: $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$ — $= \dfrac{4\sin x\cos^2 x}{2\cos^2 x}$
Mark 6: Answer — $= 2\sin x$

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, the graphs of $f(x) = 2\sin 2x$ and $g(x) = -\cos(x + 45^\circ)$ are drawn for the interval $x \in [0^\circ\,;\,180^\circ]$. $A(105^\circ\,;\,-1)$ lies on $f$.

Write down the period of $f$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark):
Mark 1: Period $= 180^\circ$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the range of $g$ in the interval $x \in [0^\circ\,;\,180^\circ]$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Lower bound $-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$
Mark 2: Range — $y \in \left[-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,;\,1\right]$ (i.e. $-0{,}71 \leq y \leq 1$)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the values of $x$, in the interval $x \in [0^\circ\,;\,180^\circ]$, for which $f(x)\cdot g(x) > 0$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Marks 1–2 (double mark): $x \in (45^\circ\,;\,90^\circ)$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the values of $x$, in the interval $x \in [0^\circ\,;\,180^\circ]$, for which $f(x) + 1 \leq 0$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Marks 1–2 (double mark): $f(x) \leq -1$, so $x \in [105^\circ\,;\,165^\circ]$

subQuestions.questionText: Another graph $p$ is defined as $p(x) = -f(x)$. $D(k\,;\,-1)$ lies on $p$. Determine the value(s) of $k$ in the interval $x \in [0^\circ\,;\,180^\circ]$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Reading off — $p(x) = -2\sin 2x$, so $-2\sin 2x = -1$ (i.e. $2\sin 2x = 1$)
Mark 2: $k = 15^\circ$
Mark 3: $k = 75^\circ$

subQuestions.questionText: Graph $h$ is obtained when $g$ is translated $45^\circ$ to the left. Determine the equation of $h$. Write your answer in its simplest form.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $h(x) = -\cos(x + 90^\circ)$
Mark 2: Answer — $h(x) = \sin x$

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, $S$, $T$ and $K$ lie in the same horizontal plane. $RS$ is a vertical tower. The angle of depression from $R$ to $K$ is $\beta$. $T\hat{S}K = \alpha$, $TS = p$ metres and the area of $\triangle STK$ is $q$ m$^2$.

Determine the length of $SK$ in terms of $p$, $q$ and $\alpha$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Substitution into the area formula — $q = \dfrac{1}{2}p(SK)\sin\alpha$
Mark 2: Answer — $SK = \dfrac{2q}{p\sin\alpha}$

subQuestions.questionText: Show that $RS = \dfrac{2q\tan\beta}{p\sin\alpha}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: $R\hat{K}S = \beta$ (angle of depression = alternate angle)
Mark 2: Correct trig ratio — $\dfrac{RS}{SK} = \tan\beta \Rightarrow RS = SK\tan\beta = \dfrac{2q\tan\beta}{p\sin\alpha}$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the size of $\alpha$ if $\alpha < 90^\circ$ and $RS = 70$ m, $p = 80$ m, $q = 2\,500$ m$^2$ and $\beta = 42^\circ$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: Correct substitution into $RS$ — $70 = \dfrac{2(2500)\tan 42^\circ}{80\sin\alpha}$
Mark 2: Value of $\sin\alpha$ — $\sin\alpha = \dfrac{25}{28}\tan 42^\circ = 0{,}80\ldots$
Mark 3: Answer — $\alpha = 53{,}51^\circ$

subQuestions.questionText: In the diagram, $O$ is the centre of the circle, with $K$, $T$ and $P$ on the circumference. Use the diagram to prove the theorem which states that the angle subtended by a chord at the centre of the circle is equal to twice the angle subtended by the same chord at the circumference, that is, prove that $T\hat{O}P = 2T\hat{K}P$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1: Construction — draw $KO$ produced
Mark 2: $\hat{O}_1 = \hat{K}_1 + \hat{T}$ [ext $\angle$ of $\triangle$]; but $\hat{K}_1 = \hat{T}$ [$\angle$s opp equal sides] so $\hat{O}_1 = 2\hat{K}_1$
Mark 3: $\hat{O}_2 = \hat{K}_2 + \hat{P}$ [ext $\angle$ of $\triangle$]; but $\hat{K}_2 = \hat{P}$ [$\angle$s opp equal sides] so $\hat{O}_2 = 2\hat{K}_2$
Mark 4: $\hat{O}_1 + \hat{O}_2 = 2\hat{K}_1 + 2\hat{K}_2 = 2(\hat{K}_1 + \hat{K}_2)$
Mark 5: $\therefore T\hat{O}P = 2T\hat{K}P$

subQuestions.questionText: In the diagram, $O$ is the centre of the circle and $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. $OB$ and $OD$ are drawn. If $\hat{O}_1 = 4x + 100^\circ$ and $\hat{C} = x + 34^\circ$, calculate, giving reasons, the size of $x$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $\hat{A} = 2x + 50^\circ$
Mark 2 (R): [$\angle$ at centre $= 2\times\angle$ at circumference]
Mark 3 (S): $x + 34^\circ + 2x + 50^\circ = 180^\circ$
Mark 4 (R): [opp $\angle$s of cyclic quad]
Mark 5: $3x = 96^\circ \Rightarrow x = 32^\circ$

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, $O$ is the centre of the larger circle. $OB$ is a diameter of the smaller circle. Chord $AB$ of the larger circle intersects the smaller circle at $M$ and $B$.

Write down the size of $O\hat{M}B$. Provide a reason.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $O\hat{M}B = 90^\circ$
Mark 2 (R): [$\angle$ in semi-circle]

subQuestions.questionText: If $AB = \sqrt{300}$ units and $OM = 5$ units, calculate, giving reasons, the length of $OB$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $AB = \sqrt{300} = 10\sqrt{3}$, so $MB = 5\sqrt{3}$
Mark 2 (R): [line from centre $\perp$ to chord]
Mark 3 (S): $OB^2 = OM^2 + MB^2 = 5^2 + (5\sqrt{3})^2$ [Pythagoras]
Mark 4: Answer — $OB = 10$ units

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, $ABCD$ is a parallelogram with $AB = 14$ units. $AD$ is produced to $E$ such that $AD:DE = 4:3$. $EB$ intersects $DC$ in $F$. $EB = 21$ units.

Calculate, with reasons, the length of $FB$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $\dfrac{FB}{EB} = \dfrac{DA}{EA}$
Mark 2 (R): [prop theorem; $DC \parallel AB$ / line $\parallel$ one side of $\triangle$]
Mark 3: $FB = \dfrac{4p \times 21}{7p} = 12$ units

subQuestions.questionText: Prove, with reasons, that $\triangle EDF \;|||\; \triangle EAB$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): In $\triangle EDF$ and $\triangle EAB$: $\hat{E}$ is common
Mark 2 (S/R): $E\hat{D}F = \hat{A}$ [corresp $\angle$s; $EA \parallel CB$]
Mark 3 (S or R): $E\hat{F}D = E\hat{B}A$ [corresp $\angle$s; $DC \parallel AB$], $\therefore \triangle EDF \;|||\; \triangle EAB$ [$\angle;\angle;\angle$]

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate, with reasons, the length of $FC$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $\dfrac{DF}{AB} = \dfrac{ED}{EA}$ [$||| \triangle$s]
Mark 2: $DF = \dfrac{3p \times 14}{7p} = 6$ units
Mark 3: $FC = 14 - DF = 8$ units [$DC = AB = 14$ units; opp sides of $\parallel^m$]

subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, $PQRS$ is a cyclic quadrilateral such that $PQ = PR$. The tangents to the circle through $P$ and $R$ meet $QS$ produced at $A$. $RS$ is produced to meet tangent $AP$ at $B$. $PS$ is produced to meet tangent $AR$ at $C$. $PR$ and $QS$ intersect at $M$.

Prove, giving reasons, that $\hat{S}_3 = \hat{S}_4$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $\hat{S}_3 = P\hat{Q}R$ [ext $\angle$ of cyclic quad]
Mark 2 (R): reason as above
Mark 3 (S/R): $\hat{R}_3 = P\hat{Q}R$ [$\angle$s opp equal sides], so $\hat{S}_3 = \hat{R}_3$
Mark 4 (S): But $\hat{S}_4 = \hat{R}_3$ [$\angle$s in the same seg]
Mark 5 (R): $\therefore \hat{S}_3 = \hat{S}_4$

subQuestions.questionText: Prove, giving reasons, that $SMRC$ is a cyclic quadrilateral.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1 (S): $\hat{R}_1 + \hat{R}_2 = P\hat{Q}R$ [tan chord theorem]
Mark 2 (R): reason as above
Mark 3 (S): $\hat{S}_4 = P\hat{Q}R$ [proved in 10.1], so $\hat{S}_4 = \hat{R}_1 + \hat{R}_2$
Mark 4 (R): $\therefore SMRC$ is a cyclic quad [converse ext $\angle$ of cyclic quad]

subQuestions.questionText: Prove, giving reasons, that $RP$ is a tangent to the circle passing through $P$, $S$ and $A$ at $P$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (6 marks):
Mark 1 (S/R): $\hat{S}_3 = \hat{R}_2 + \hat{P}_2$ [ext $\angle$ of $\triangle$]
Mark 2 (S): $\hat{S}_4 = \hat{P}_1 + \hat{A}_2$ [ext $\angle$ of $\triangle$], so $\hat{R}_2 + \hat{P}_2 = \hat{A}_2 + \hat{P}_1$
Mark 3 (S/R): But $\hat{P}_1 = \hat{R}_2$ [tan chord theorem]
Mark 4: $\therefore \hat{P}_2 = \hat{A}_2$
Mark 5 (R): $\therefore RP$ is a tangent to the circle passing through $P$, $S$ and $A$ [converse tan chord theorem / converse alt seg theorem]
Mark 6: consistency mark
(Alternatively, in $\triangle MSP$ and $\triangle MPA$ using $AR = AP$ [tans from same point] and sum of $\angle$s in $\triangle$.)
